records.text: On May 20, 2023, the assistant explained that legal risks when businesses use third-party vendors or contractors depend on the contract, services, and applicable laws. Potential risks include liability for vendor errors or unlawful conduct, regulatory-compliance failures, unclear intellectual-property ownership, mishandling of confidential information, and contractual disputes.

The assistant gave a payroll example of possible business liability: a payroll vendor fails to withhold taxes or remit them to the government on time, and the employer company is fined by the IRS. The assistant said the employer may remain liable because tax compliance ultimately rests with the employer; contractual compliance or indemnification terms may not remove all responsibility. The assistant recommended monitoring the vendor and ensuring tax obligations are met.

The assistant recommended managing vendor and contractor legal risks by conducting due diligence and risk assessments; using written contracts with clear payment, service, confidentiality, dispute-resolution, and termination terms; monitoring performance through reports, audits, or site visits; training employees and vendors; protecting sensitive data; considering insurance; and consulting legal professionals. The assistant said these measures can reduce, but not eliminate, legal risk, and businesses should prepare contingency plans.

The assistant identified industry-specific requirements for third-party vendors: healthcare vendors handling protected health information must comply with HIPAA and sign a Business Associate Agreement; financial businesses must comply with GLBA safeguards for financial information; and vendors processing payment cards must meet PCI DSS requirements. The assistant said businesses may need additional contract terms, certifications, or attestations.

In response to a request for recent examples, the assistant cited three data-breach cases: Capital One’s 2019 breach, attributed to a firewall configuration error involving a third-party vendor, followed by lawsuits and regulatory fines including an $80 million settlement with the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency; Target’s 2013 breach affecting more than 40 million customers, attributed to a vulnerability in third-party vendor software, followed by a $10 million customer settlement and more than $100 million in legal fees and costs; and Uber’s 2017 breach affecting 57 million customers and drivers, attributed to a hacker accessing third-party vendor code on an open-source platform, followed by a $148 million settlement. These were examples as presented by the assistant.
entities: U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

On 2023-05-29, the user asked for a summary of WIRED’s YouTube video “A.I. Tries 20 Jobs.” The video had professionals test AI on tasks from their fields. AI generated a usable craft-beer website from code and produced a plausible initial response to a medical question, but the doctor cautioned that its advice was limited and not a substitute for professional care. Other testers found AI outputs generic, inaccurate, inconsistent, or lacking human judgment: examples included awkward logo text, relationship advice that was hard to act on, a weak legal memo, unnatural news narration and translation, an uncreative cocktail, and an incorrect workout plan. Creative professionals saw some value in AI for brainstorming or as a starting point, but not as a replacement for their expertise; the chef noted that its recipe came close but missed yogurt and risked drying out the chicken. The DJ also found a recommended song that appeared not to exist. Overall, the participants were generally skeptical that AI could do their jobs well, though some were impressed or unsettled by its capabilities.
